drivers.driver: The institutional culture failed, resulting in widespread misconduct that has proven difficult and expensive to remediate [D01, D05].
Long-term earnings power is structurally impaired by ongoing regulatory restrictions on asset growth [D03, D07].
The bank's competitive advantage in customer retention has been damaged, rendering the future of the deposit franchise unknowable [D01].
Management turnover and the necessity of massive trust repair absorb capital and focus, diverting resources from core banking activities [D01, D05].

final.memo:
When we invest in a bank, we look for a low-cost deposit franchise and sound, disciplined management. In this instance, the culture that allowed widespread sales-practices failures demonstrated a profound breakdown in the internal controls we require [D01]. This is not merely a cyclical downturn or a temporary setback; it is an institutional failure that has made the future of the bank's earning power unknowable [D01, D05].

The Federal Reserve's asset-growth restriction serves as a tangible marker of this deterioration, placing a ceiling on the bank's ability to operate effectively [D03, D07]. While others may look at a discount to tangible book value as an opportunity, we must be honest with ourselves: a cheap price does not cure an impaired business [D04, D06]. The costs of remediation, litigation, and trust repair create a persistent drag that complicates the normalization of earnings [D03, D05].

We have long held this position, but when the facts change, we must change our minds [D07]. We do not anchor on our cost basis or hope for a recovery that is no longer supported by the business's fundamentals [D04]. The institutional imperative for growth and the integrity of the deposit franchise have been fundamentally compromised, and it is time to move on [D01].
